sessions.title: Active Learning and Critical Thinking
sessions.content:
What does Active Learning look like?

Teachers:

  • Encourage students to ask and answer questions
  • Allow students to share and explore ideas
  • Guide students to connect learning to their own experiences, prior learning, and the real world
  • Challenge students to use higher order thinking skills
  • Encourage students to seek information and figure out problems on their own
  • Teach students specific active learning strategies
  • Avoid lectures and telling students what to do

Students:

  • Are engaged in activities (reading, thinking, writing, doing projects)
  • Ask and answer questions
  • Connect learning to their own experiences, prior learning, and the real world
  • Explore their own attitudes and values
  • Use higher order thinking skills (analysis, synthesis, evaluation)
  • Know how to find information
  • Solve problems
  • Use feedback from teachers and other students to complete learning and improve performance.

sessions.title: Critical Thinking in Detail
sessions.content:
Critical Thinking in Detail

Critical thinking is the intellectually disciplined process of actively and skillfully conceptualizing, applying, analyzing, synthesizing, and/or evaluating information gathered from, or generated by, observation, experience, reflection, reasoning, or communication.

Key Components (Higher Order Thinking):

  • Analyzing: Breaking information into parts to explore understandings and relationships (comparing, contrasting, categorizing).
  • Evaluating: Justifying a decision or course of action based on specific criteria and standards (checking, critiquing, judging).
  • Synthesizing/Creating: Putting elements together to form a coherent or functional whole; reorganizing elements into a new pattern (designing, constructing, planning, producing).

Question Stems to Encourage Critical Thinking:

  • What evidence supports your claim?
  • How would you solve this problem differently?
  • What are the potential biases in this information?
  • How is this connected to what we learned previously?
  • What would happen if...?

The Critical Thinking Process:

  1. Identify the issue: What is the real problem or question?
  2. Gather information: Seek relevant facts and evidence.
  3. Evaluate evidence: Determine the reliability and validity of the sources.
  4. Consider viewpoints: Analyze different perspectives.
  5. Draw conclusions: Make a reasoned judgment based on the evidence.
  6. Communicate findings: Explain the reasoning clearly.

sessions.title: Transform Questions
sessions.content:
Transform Questions

Closed QuestionOpen Question
Where is the Jungle Book set?Why do you think the author chose that setting, and how does it impact the characters?
What does the circulatory system do?How does the circulatory system work with other body systems to keep the body functioning?
Find the perimeter of this rectangle.How can you prove that your method for finding the perimeter works for all rectangles?
How many sides does a rectangle have?What are the defining properties of a rectangle, and how do they differ from other quadrilaterals?
Find 3+4, 5+2, 1+6.What patterns do you notice in these equations? Can you create a new set of equations that follow the same rule?

sessions.title: Active Learning Strategies
sessions.content:
Active Learning Strategies

Conscience Alley: An activity in which one child takes on the role of a character while the other children create each side of an alley, putting forth their opposing views on the character's dilemma as the child in role walks between them. The character listens to his or her 'conscience' before making a decision about the course of action to take.

Hot-Seating: A drama activity in which a child takes on the role of a character in the 'hot seat', while the other children ask the character prepared or improvised questions.

Rainbow: An idea-sharing technique: discussion is paused and group members are given colours. They form new groups of children with the same colour and share their ideas.

Snowballing: An activity in which pairs discuss a subject and then join with another pair to form a group and share ideas. Two groups then join together and so on, until there is a whole-class discussion.

Thought Tracking: An activity in which the action in a story (such as a Role Play) is frozen at a key moment and the thoughts of a character are spoken aloud, either by a child in role or by a group.

Walking Bus: An activity in which music is played while the children walk around the classroom. When the music stops, the teacher asks a question that the children discuss with those nearest to them.

sessions.content:
We remember

  • 10% of what we read
  • 20% of what we hear
  • 30% of what we see
  • 50% of what we see and hear
  • 70% of what we discuss with others
  • 80% of what we personally experience
  • 95% of what we teach others

Edgar Dale, Audio-Visual Methods in Teaching (3rd Edition) (New York: Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1969).

sessions.title: World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025
sessions.content:
World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025

According to the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025, employers identified the following as the 11 most important core skills for workers in 2025. The ranking is based on the percentage of employers surveyed who consider each skill a core skill for their workforce.

RankSkillEmployers identifying it as a core skill
1Analytical thinking69%
2Resilience, flexibility and agility67%
3Leadership and social influence61%
4Creative thinking57%
5Motivation and self-awareness52%
6Technological literacy51%
7Empathy and active listening50%
8Curiosity and lifelong learning50%
9Talent management47%
10Service orientation and customer service47%
11AI and big data45%
